b: Cause: long-term exposure to irritants : tobacco smoke (commonest) , biomass fuel smoke (wood, charcoal: very important in Kenya) , occupational dusts and fumes, air pollution; recurrent infection.

Pathology: mucous gland hypertrophy and goblet cell hyperplasia (increased Reid index above 0.5), mucus hypersecretion, chronic inflammation, ciliary dysfunction , bronchial wall thickening and airway narrowing.
Chronic productive cough , worse in the morning ; recurrent exacerbations with purulent sputum, wheeze and breathlessness .
Signs: coarse crackles and rhonchi, wheeze, cyanosis and fluid retention (cor pulmonale) in advanced disease (" blue bloater ": overweight, cyanosed, hypoxic, oedematous, CO2 retention).
Spirometry ( post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.7 = COPD); chest X-ray (increased bronchovascular markings, to exclude other causes); sputum culture in exacerbations; FBC (polycythaemia), ABG .
Defined clinically : Persistent productive cough for at least 3 consecutive months in at least 2 consecutive years .
Common in cigarette smokers and urban dwellers, affecting 20–25% of men aged 40–65.
A distinctive feature is hypersecretion of mucus beginning in the large airways .
Cigarette smoking is the most important cause, along with irritants like sulfur dioxide and nitrogen dioxide.
Irritants lead to hypertrophy of mucous glands in the trachea and bronchi, and an increase in goblet cells in smaller bronchi and bronchioles.
Clinical Definition: Productive cough for 3 months in 2 consecutive years
Morphology: Hypertrophy of mucus-secreting glands ( Reid index 0.4 ) + goblet cell metaplasia

Chronic bronchitis: a clinical diagnosis: productive cough on most days for at least 3 months in each of 2 consecutive years, with other causes excluded.

Submucosal mucous glands (seromucous) – located in the larger bronchi; normal Reid index ≈ 0.4.: Chronic irritation causes gland hypertrophy → Reid index > 0.5, the hallmark of chronic bronchitis; explains persistent mucus hypersecretion.
Chronic bronchitis: goblet cell and mucous gland hypertrophy, airway inflammation (neutrophils, macrophages, CD8 T cells), luminal narrowing.
"Pink puffer" (emphysema: breathless, thin, no cyanosis) versus "blue bloater" (chronic bronchitis: cyanosed, oedematous): a descriptive pair, with most patients having a mixture.
Hyper‑reactivity here produces occupational asthma and chronic bronchitis.

qs.q: How is chronic bronchitis clinically defined for diagnostic purposes?
o: Permanent bronchial dilation accompanied by severe cartilage destruction
Persistent productive cough for at least 3 months in 2 consecutive years
Reversible bronchospasm triggered exclusively by environmental allergens
Progressive dyspnea associated with a Usual Interstitial Pneumonia pattern
qs.e: Chronic bronchitis requires a clinical definition of a persistent productive cough lasting at least 3 months within 2 consecutive years. Asthma involves reversible bronchospasm, and bronchiectasis involves permanent dilation.

qs.q: What is the specific diagnostic criterion for chronic bronchitis regarding symptom duration?
o: Any chronic cough accompanied by recurrent wheezing for one full year
Daily productive cough lasting continuously for at least six months duration
Intermittent morning cough with phlegm over a period of six weeks duration
Cough and sputum on most days for at least three consecutive months
qs.e: Chronic bronchitis is clinically defined as cough and sputum on most days for at least 3 consecutive months for at least 2 successive years. This distinguishes it from acute or transient bronchitis.

qs.q: Which pathological feature distinguishes chronic bronchitis from emphysema?
o: Destruction of alveolar septae by active elastase
Increased Reid index from mucous gland hyperplasia
Reduced elastic recoil of lung parenchymal tissue
Permanent airspace enlargement distal to terminal bronchioles
qs.e: Chronic bronchitis is characterized by mucous gland hyperplasia leading to an increased Reid index. Emphysema involves alveolar destruction and a loss of elastic recoil rather than glandular hypertrophy.

qs.q: A patient with long-standing chronic bronchitis and emphysema develops right ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure. What is recognized as the commonest cause of this secondary cardiac condition?
o: Left-sided heart failure
Primary pulmonary hypertension
Chronic lung disease
Pulmonary valve stenosis
qs.e: Cor pulmonale, characterized by right ventricular hypertrophy and heart failure, is most commonly caused by chronic lung disease leading to pulmonary hypertension. Left-sided heart failure typically causes left ventricular or bilateral strain rather than isolated cor pulmonale.

qs.q: A mucolytic agent is administered to a patient with chronic bronchitis to break down disulfide bonds in glycoproteins via its reducing sulfhydryl group. What is this drug?
o: Ammonium chloride
Pseudoephedrine
N-Acetylcysteine
Steam inhalation
qs.e: N-Acetylcysteine breaks down S-S bonds in glycoproteins through its reducing SH group to decrease mucous viscosity. Ammonium chloride is an expectorant that stimulates respiratory fluid production.

qs.q: A 45-year-old man with chronic bronchitis is prescribed an inhaled agent that reduces sputum thickness. What is the primary molecular mechanism of this drug?
o: Stimulation of neutral sialomucin synthesis
Osmotic drawing of water into the airway lumen
Reduction of glycoprotein disulfide bonds
Cleavage of extracellular bacterial DNA strands
qs.e: N-Acetylcysteine exerts its mucolytic action by using its free sulfhydryl group to break disulfide bonds within mucus glycoproteins. Hypertonic saline acts via osmotic water influx, whereas dornase alfa targets extracellular DNA.

qs.q: A 58-year-old male heavy smoker presents with a chronic cough and recurrent expectoration. For him to meet the clinical definition of chronic bronchitis, what is the minimum duration requirement for his symptoms?
o: Most days for at least 6 months a year for 3 successive years
Intermittent cough for at least 1 month a year for 3 successive years
Every day for at least 6 consecutive months for 1 year
Most days for at least 3 months a year for 2 successive years
qs.e: Chronic bronchitis is defined clinically by chronic or recurrent expectoration present on most days for a minimum of 3 months a year for at least 2 successive years. Other durations do not fit this specific diagnostic criterion.

qs.q: The Reid index in chronic bronchitis is
o: Ratio of FEV1 to FVC on spirometry
Ratio of goblet cells to ciliated cells in epithelium
Ratio of alveolar wall thickness to capillary diameter
Ratio of submucosal gland thickness to bronchial wall thickness
qs.e: The Reid index measures submucosal gland layer thickness divided by bronchial wall thickness. Normal is ≤0.4; chronic bronchitis exceeds 0.4 due to gland hypertrophy.

es.q: Compare and contrast the pathological features of Emphysema and Chronic Bronchitis.
es.m:
- **Emphysema Site and Mechanism**: Affects the alveoli and acinus through a protease-antiprotease imbalance, where unchecked elastase destroys alveolar septae and leads to a loss of elastic recoil and air trapping.
- **Chronic Bronchitis Site and Definition**: Affects the bronchi, clinically defined as a productive cough for greater than three months per year over two consecutive years.
- **Bronchitis Mechanism**: Characterised by mucus gland hyperplasia, indicated by an increased Reid index.
- **Emphysema Clinical Phenotype**: Associated with the pink puffer presentation, characterised by thin build, dyspnoea, and compensatory hyperventilation.

es.q: Define chronic bronchitis and detail its specific diagnostic criteria.
es.m:
- **Clinical Definition:** Defined strictly by clinical features rather than purely by structural or radiological changes.
- **Expectoration:** Characterized by chronic or recurrent expectoration, meaning coughing up lots of sputum.
- **Frequency:** The symptom must be present on most days.
- **Duration:** Must persist for a minimum of 3 months a year.
- **Timeframe:** Must occur for at least 2 successive years, which serves as a clinical warning.

es.q: A pathologist is reviewing a lung biopsy from a patient with a long history of heavy smoking and chronic cough. Upon microscopic examination, the pathologist measures the Reid Index. a) What specific anatomical feature does the Reid Index quantify? b) What value of the Reid Index is considered indic
es.m: a) The Reid Index measures submucosal gland hypertrophy in the bronchial wall. b) A Reid Index greater than 0.4 indicates significant enlargement, characteristic of chronic bronchitis.

es.q: A medical student asks about the significance of the Reid Index in chronic bronchitis. Briefly explain what the Reid Index measures and what value indicates significant pathological change.
es.m: The Reid Index measures the degree of submucosal gland hypertrophy in chronic bronchitis (3 marks). A Reid Index value greater than 0.4 indicates significant enlargement (2 marks).

ai.subject: Pathology
ai.summary: Chronic bronchitis is a form of COPD defined by a productive cough for ≥3 months in ≥2 consecutive years, caused by long‑term airway irritation. Mucous‑gland hypertrophy and goblet‑cell hyperplasia narrow airways and produce excess mucus.

sections.p: A clinical diagnosis of chronic bronchitis requires a productive cough on most days for at least three months in two consecutive years, after excluding asthma, infection, and heart failure.
b: Reid index >0.5 on histology confirms mucous‑gland hypertrophy
Post‑bronchodilator FEV1/FVC <0.70 indicates COPD

t.b: Does the patient have airflow obstruction? A reduced FEV1/FVC (<0.70) confirms COPD, supporting chronic bronchitis.
Are there alternative diagnoses (e.g., pneumonia, heart failure)? Look for increased bronchovascular markings; a normal film does not rule out disease.
Is a bacterial infection driving the current flare? Growth of typical pathogens (H. influenzae, S. pneumoniae) guides antibiotic use.

sections.p: Severity is staged by GOLD grades using post‑bronchodilator FEV1 % predicted, and by symptom burden (mMRC dyspnoea scale or CAT score).
b: GOLD 1: FEV1 ≥80% (mild)
GOLD 2: 50–79% (moderate)
GOLD 3: 30–49% (severe)
GOLD 4: <30% (very severe)

sections.p: Chronic irritation of the bronchial epithelium drives glandular hyperplasia and mucus over‑production.
b: Cigarette smoke (most common worldwide)
Biomass fuel smoke (wood, charcoal – major in low‑resource settings)
Occupational dusts/fumes (grain, cotton, silica)
Ambient air pollution (SO₂, NO₂)
Recurrent lower‑respiratory infections (including TB in endemic areas)

sections.p: Patients report a daily productive cough, especially in the morning, with sputum that may become purulent during exacerbations. Over time dyspnoea, wheeze, and cyanosis develop.
b: Coarse crackles and rhonchi on auscultation
Peripheral oedema and jugular venous distension in advanced disease (cor pulmonale)
‘Blue bloater’ phenotype: overweight, cyanosed, CO₂ retention

sections.p: Tests confirm airflow limitation, assess severity, and identify treatable triggers.

t.b: Is there hypoxaemia or hypercapnia? Low PaO₂ or high PaCO₂ signals need for supplemental O₂ or ventilation support.
Is polycythaemia present? Elevated haematocrit reflects chronic hypoxia and may guide oxygen therapy.
Can peak expiratory flow (PEF) be measured? A reduced PEF suggests obstruction, though less precise than spirometry.

sections.p: Complications arise from chronic hypoxia, inflammation, and frequent infections.
b: Acute exacerbation with fever, increased sputum purulence, or rapid dyspnoea
Cor pulmonale (right‑heart failure)
Respiratory failure requiring ventilation
Pulmonary hypertension

sections.p: Treat the irritant exposure, control inflammation, and prevent or treat exacerbations.
b: Smoking cessation (counselling, nicotine replacement, varenicline) – stops disease progression
Vaccination (influenza, pneumococcal) – reduces infection‑driven exacerbations
Long‑acting bronchodilators (LABA or LAMA) – improve airflow and symptoms
Inhaled corticosteroids for frequent exacerbators – lower inflammation, avoid in mild disease due to pneumonia risk
Pulmonary rehabilitation – enhances exercise tolerance
O₂ therapy for PaO₂ <55 mmHg or SaO₂ <88% – prevents cor pulmonale

sections.p: Regular review monitors lung function, symptom control, and comorbidities.
b: Spirometry every 12 months (or sooner after exacerbation)
Assess smoking status and reinforce cessation
Screen for depression and anxiety, common in chronic disease
Educate on early recognition of exacerbation signs

sections.p: Conditions sharing cough and dyspnoea can mislead diagnosis.
b: Asthma – reversible obstruction, often younger onset, eosinophilia
Bronchiectasis – localized dilated bronchi, frequent purulent sputum, CT changes
Heart failure – orthopnoea, peripheral oedema, cardiomegaly on X‑ray

sections.p: Certain findings may appear normal despite disease.
b: Normal chest X‑ray early in disease – does not exclude chronic bronchitis
Spirometry may be within normal limits during a symptom‑free period; repeat if suspicion persists
Sputum culture can be negative in viral‑driven exacerbations

whenToSeekHelp: Sudden worsening of breathlessness or chest tightness
New fever, chills, or purulent sputum
Swelling of ankles or sudden weight gain

faq.q: Why does chronic bronchitis cause cyanosis?
faq.a: Mucus plugging and airway narrowing impair gas exchange, leading to low oxygen (hypoxaemia) that makes the skin appear bluish.

faq.q: Can a non‑smoker develop chronic bronchitis?
faq.a: Yes; prolonged exposure to biomass fuel smoke, occupational dusts, or severe air pollution can cause the same airway changes.
Airflow limitation is largely irreversible, but quitting irritants and using bronchodilators can improve symptoms and slow progression.
